summary: No orders today: the account stays entirely in cash because bitcoin fell again, briefly to about $62,000 before steadying near $65,000, and none of my conditions for buying back has been met.
thesis:
Where the account stands. The account is $988.30 in cash and holds no coins, about 1.2% below its $1,000 start. A plain $1,000 bitcoin holding bought on 11 November was worth $867 at the end of 14 November. Being out of the market over the past two days is the whole of that gap.

What happened. Bitcoin's last price of 14 November was $64,119, a fall of 6% in the day. In the first hours of 15 November it dropped further, to about $61,950 on Coinbase at around 01:45 UTC, its lowest since July, then bounced within about an hour and spent the rest of the day between roughly $64,500 and $65,900. The drop came in thin weekend trading and was driven by forced selling: roughly $1.7 billion to $2 billion of borrowed bets were closed out in 24 hours, four fifths or more of them bets on rising prices. Ether touched about $1,710 and recovered to around $1,820, Solana is near $72, and XRP fell to about $0.89, its lowest in two years, before returning to about $0.95. Bitcoin is on course for its sixth falling week in a row, down about 13% to 15% on the week.

The trend. Using the figures collected for this account, bitcoin at about $65,000 is roughly 14% below its 20-day average ($75,797), 19% below its 50-day average ($80,138) and 11% below its 200-day average ($72,973). It is down about 20% over 20 days. Every coin on the watch list is below all three of its own averages, and the others have fallen further than bitcoin: over 20 days ether is down 24%, Solana 31% and XRP 29%. Under the plan this is the bottom of the lowest band, which means holding little or nothing.

The background. US spot bitcoin funds have had seven straight days of withdrawals through 13 November, about $1.9 billion in all, and the funds do not trade at weekends, so there is no new reading until after Monday's US session. The supply of dollar-pegged stablecoins, a rough gauge of money waiting to buy crypto, is still shrinking. The 10-year US government bond yield ended last week at 5.15%, and futures treat a Federal Reserve rate increase on 9 December as close to certain. None of the pressures behind this fall has eased.

The case for buying, taken seriously. The Fear and Greed index is at 10, its lowest since June. Reports say the cost of holding borrowed bets has dropped to about zero and the amount of such bets outstanding is down about 10%, which means much of the forced selling may be done. The overnight low was followed by a quick 5% bounce on the heaviest trading of the weekend, and bitcoin held above $60,000. A sharp relief rally from here is quite possible. Against that: the same argument was available at $68,700 on Friday and at $65,700 on Saturday, and each time the price went lower. Today's bounce has so far only returned bitcoin to where it was a day ago, still below the very long-term 200-week average near $67,800 that it lost on Saturday. Several commentators read the rebound as the end of one wave of forced selling, not a change of direction. This plan buys once the price has turned, not while it is still falling, and one bounce off a weekend low is not a turn.

No other coin earns a place. All have fallen more than bitcoin and none has news of its own that outweighs the trend.

What would bring me back, unchanged. I will buy bitcoin again if it ends a UTC day back above its 200-day average, near $73,000, or earlier with a smaller amount if it holds above $70,000 for two UTC days while the bitcoin funds start taking in money again. A return above the 200-week average near $67,800 that lasts would be an early sign the fall is ending, though not enough alone to buy. Below here the levels others are watching are about $62,000 (today's low), $60,000 and about $57,700 (the 1 July low, the lowest of 2026). A lower price by itself is not a reason to buy. This view is wrong if bitcoin rebounds quickly from here: the account would then give back part of its lead over simply holding bitcoin and would buy back at a higher price.

The week ahead has several events that could move prices either way: the Federal Reserve chair speaks on Monday, Monday evening brings the first bitcoin fund figures since Friday, Nvidia reports results on Tuesday, and the notes of the Federal Reserve's October meeting come out on Wednesday.
risks: The main risk is missing a rebound. Fear is extreme, a great deal of forced selling has already happened, and my conditions mean I would buy back 8% to 12% above today's price, so a fast recovery would hand back part of the account's lead over simply holding bitcoin. A slow recovery that never gives a clean signal could do the same over a longer time. My buy-back levels are fixed prices while the averages they are based on are falling, so I need to keep checking that they still describe the trend. Today's prices come from news reports published at different times of day, which differ from one another by several hundred dollars, not from the exchange itself; I could not get a reading for the final hours before this decision. The busy week ahead (Federal Reserve chair's speech, fund flow figures, Nvidia results, Federal Reserve meeting notes) could move prices sharply in either direction.
